script.opening: "I keep getting these horrendous attacks of being sick — vomiting for a day or two with bad stomach pain — every few weeks. I’ve been to A&E loads, had scans and bloods, all normal. The weird thing is the ONLY thing that helps is standing in a really hot shower for ages — I almost live in there during an attack. What’s wrong with me?"

facts.text: For about 9 months, every 3–4 weeks. Feels sick in the morning, then vomits many times a day for 1–2 days, with cramping pain across the tummy. Then fine in between, "pretty much". Last attack ended 4 days ago.
Stands in a very hot shower for hours during attacks — "the only thing that helps". Once got a red scald on his back.
No blood in the vomit, not green. No weight loss to speak of. No fever, no jaundice, no headache in the mornings, no swallowing difficulty. Bowels normal. Passing urine normally between attacks.

Pauses, then: "I smoke weed, yeah. Most days." Started at 16; for the last 2 years about 3–4 joints a day, stronger stuff. "Nobody at the hospital asked." Thinks it helps the nausea. Drinks at weekends, about 10 units. No other drugs. Smokes 10 cigarettes a day.
No medicines; given anti-sickness tablets in A&E "which didn’t really help". No allergies. No diabetes.
Works in a warehouse; has had a warning for missed days. Lives with his girlfriend. Drives a car to work.

Frustrated and a bit defensive about hospitals not finding anything. Reveal the cannabis only if asked in a non-judgemental way; if lectured, shut down ("I knew you’d go on about that"). Push back: "But it helps me feel less sick." Ambivalent about stopping but willing to take details of support.

ice.ideas: "They’re missing something serious — an ulcer or something."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of losing his job, and worry about being judged for cannabis; also worried about getting into trouble with the police or his employer if it’s written down.
ice.expectations: "A test that finds what’s wrong, or a tablet that stops it."

cues: "The only thing that helps is standing in a really hot shower" — the key clue.
"Nobody at the hospital asked" (once cannabis is disclosed) — he will talk if asked without judgement.
"But it helps me feel less sick" — the misconception to address with the cessation message.

checkpoints.text: Recognises CANNABIS HYPEREMESIS SYNDROME — cyclical vomiting/abdominal pain in a chronic cannabis user, classically relieved by HOT bathing, with multiple normal prior investigations
Takes a NON-JUDGEMENTAL substance/cannabis history (frequency/duration/amount), recognising CHS is frequently missed because cannabis is not asked about
Excludes other causes of cyclical vomiting and red flags (GI obstruction/pancreatitis, raised ICP, metabolic/endocrine — DKA/Addisonian, pregnancy in women)
Delivers the CESSATION message — the only definitive treatment is cannabis cessation (resolves with abstinence, recurs with use) — clearly and supportively

Knows standard antiemetics are often poorly effective and that acute supportive care (IV fluids; topical capsaicin, an unlicensed use; other drugs chosen by the hospital team) is used acutely, and offers cessation/harm-reduction support (drug services, NICE CG51), warning about withdrawal
Asks about cannabis without judgement, addresses the patient’s distress and the "nothing’s been found" frustration, and frames cessation as the cure rather than moralising
Explains the diagnosis and the cannabis link clearly, checking understanding and engaging the patient in cessation

Safety-nets and follows up: red flags warranting reassessment, cessation support/referral, acute-episode advice (fluids, urgent care if unable to keep fluids down — dehydration/AKI; scald risk), driving law and DVLA notification, and review — recognition of CHS + the cessation message, not another scan

worked.txt: "You’ve given me a really important clue — the only thing that helps is a hot shower. That, with repeated vomiting attacks and normal scans, points strongly to a condition called cannabis hyperemesis syndrome. Can I ask — do you use cannabis, and how often?"

"No judgement at all — I ask because it’s directly relevant. Regular cannabis use can, paradoxically, cause exactly these cyclical vomiting attacks, and the hot-bath relief is almost a signature of it. It’s often missed because no one asks."
"Your previous tests being normal is reassuring, and I’ll just check there’s nothing else — any severe headaches, weight loss, or other symptoms? … No. Good."

"Here’s the key, and it’s the hard part: the only thing that truly stops this is coming off cannabis. The symptoms settle with abstinence and come back if you use again. The usual anti-sickness tablets often don’t work well for it."
"I know that’s a big ask, and I’m not here to lecture you — I’m here to help. I can refer you to a service that supports cutting down or stopping, and we’ll manage the attacks in the meantime."

"During an attack, keep hydrated and seek help if you can’t keep fluids down or get very unwell, and be careful the water isn’t hot enough to scald you. It can take weeks or longer off cannabis to settle, and you may feel irritable or sleep badly at first. And if anything new develops — severe headache, weight loss, blood — come back. But stopping cannabis is genuinely the cure here."

f.learning: CANNABIS HYPEREMESIS SYNDROME (CHS) is recurrent/CYCLICAL severe nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain in a chronic/heavy CANNABIS user, classically RELIEVED by HOT SHOWERS/BATHS (compulsive hot bathing), often after multiple normal prior investigations and A&E attendances — the hot-bathing relief being a highly characteristic clue. CHS is frequently MISSED because clinicians do not ask about cannabis, so take a non-judgemental substance history (frequency, duration, amount), normalising the question — without it the diagnosis is repeatedly missed despite extensive work-ups. Exclude other causes of cyclical/recurrent vomiting and red flags: GI causes (obstruction, peptic disease, gallstones, pancreatitis), raised intracranial pressure, metabolic/endocrine causes (DKA, Addisonian crisis, hypercalcaemia), cyclical vomiting syndrome, and pregnancy in women — reassuringly normal previous investigations plus the hot-bath/cannabis pattern support CHS, but red flags must be screened. The critical message is that the ONLY definitive treatment is CANNABIS CESSATION: symptoms resolve with abstinence and recur with continued use, so explain this clearly and supportively as the central, often-resisted point; standard antiemetics are frequently poorly effective (BNF), and acute supportive care includes IV fluids and, in acute/hospital settings, topical capsaicin to the abdomen (an unlicensed use) and other drug treatment chosen by the hospital team. Recovery with sustained abstinence may take weeks or longer. Provide harm-reduction and cessation support (motivational approach and referral to drug services, NICE CG51) for a difficult behaviour change, framing cessation as the cure rather than moralising, and warn that cannabis withdrawal (irritability, poor sleep, low appetite, low mood) can occur in the first weeks. Safety-net dehydration and electrolyte disturbance including acute kidney injury (urgent care if unable to keep fluids down) and scalds from very hot water, and cover driving: it is illegal to drive with cannabis in the blood above the specified limit or while impaired, and persistent misuse of or dependence on cannabis must be notified to the DVLA, with driving stopped. Observations and the abdomen are examined face to face, as they cannot be assessed on video. The skill is recognising the pattern (cyclical vomiting + hot-bath relief + cannabis), asking about cannabis non-judgementally, excluding red flags, and delivering the cessation message with support.

knowledge.guideline: [1] Rome IV criteria for functional gastrointestinal disorders: cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (2016) (international) · [2] NICE CG51 Drug misuse in over 16s: psychosocial interventions (2007) · [3] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: drug misuse and dependence · [4] BNF: antiemetics
knowledge.summary: Stereotyped episodes of vomiting and abdominal pain over months, repeated normal investigations, and relief from long hot showers in a regular cannabis user is cannabis hyperemesis syndrome. The diagnosis depends on asking about cannabis without judgement. Sustained cessation is the only treatment that stops the episodes.

points.t: Rome IV [1] (international) describes episodes of vomiting resembling cyclic vomiting syndrome, occurring after prolonged, excessive cannabis use, and relieved by sustained cessation. Compulsive hot bathing or showering to ease symptoms is typical. Patients are often well between episodes and have had repeated normal investigations.
The diagnosis is missed when no one asks. Ask routinely and without judgement: how often, how much, for how long, and any recent change in strength or pattern. Ask about other drugs and alcohol.

Check for red flags: bilious or bloody vomiting, severe or constant abdominal pain, weight loss, dysphagia, headache or neurological symptoms (raised intracranial pressure), jaundice. Consider diabetes (DKA), hypercalcaemia, adrenal insufficiency, pancreatitis, obstruction, peptic disease, cyclic vomiting syndrome and, in women, pregnancy. Previous normal results help, but reassess anything new.

Standard antiemetics often help little [4]. Dehydration and electrolyte disturbance, including acute kidney injury, can follow prolonged vomiting: seek urgent care if unable to keep fluids down. Warn that very hot water can scald.

Symptoms settle with sustained abstinence, which may take weeks or longer, and return with renewed use. Cannabis withdrawal (irritability, poor sleep, low appetite, low mood) can occur in the first weeks. NICE CG51 [2]: use motivational approaches and offer referral to drug treatment services.

It is illegal to drive with cannabis in the blood above a specified limit, or while impaired. DVLA [3]: persistent misuse of, or dependence on, cannabis must be notified and the person must stop driving.

model.text: Hello Mr Calland, I’m Dr Evans. What’s brought you in?

I keep getting these horrendous attacks of being sick, vomiting for a day or two with bad stomach pain, every few weeks. I’ve been to A&E loads, had scans and bloods, all normal. The weird thing is the only thing that helps is standing in a really hot shower for ages. I almost live in there during an attack. What’s wrong with me?
That sounds exhausting, and frustrating to be told everything is normal. The shower detail is really important, so thank you for mentioning it. Can I ask some questions?
model.why: Validates frustration; flags the key cue

model.text: Between the attacks, are you completely well?
Pretty much. Then it hits again.
When you vomit, is it ever green, or does it have blood in it? And is the pain ever constant and severe?
model.why: Red flags: bilious or bloody vomiting, surgical pain

model.text: No blood, not green. The pain’s bad but it goes with the sickness.
Any weight loss, trouble swallowing, headaches that wake you, or problems with your vision?
model.why: Red flags: weight loss, dysphagia, raised ICP

model.text: No, nothing like that.
Do you have diabetes or any other condition, and do you take any medicines?
No, nothing.
I ask everyone this, and there’s no judgement: do you drink alcohol or use any drugs, including cannabis?
(pauses) I smoke weed, yeah. Most days. Have done for a while. Nobody at the hospital asked.
Thank you for being honest, that really helps. Anything else, like other drugs or alcohol?
Not really.
What have you been thinking might be causing this?
I thought they were missing something serious. Weed helps me feel less sick, if anything.
How is it affecting work, and your mood?
I’ve missed a lot of days. It gets me down, but I’m okay.
Let me check your pulse, blood pressure and tummy. (Examines: observations normal, abdomen soft and non-tender, no signs of dehydration.) That’s all fine today.

Here’s what I think. The pattern you describe, with attacks every few weeks, normal tests and hot showers being the only relief, fits a condition called cannabis hyperemesis syndrome. In some people who use cannabis regularly over a long time, it starts to cause these vomiting attacks. The hot-shower relief is very typical.
model.why: Names the diagnosis with the reasoning

model.text: But it helps me feel less sick.
That’s a very common belief, and in the short term it can seem that way. With long-term regular use, it tends to do the opposite, which is why the attacks keep coming back.

The honest part is that the only thing that stops these attacks is stopping cannabis completely. It can take some weeks to settle, and the attacks come back if you start again. Anti-sickness tablets usually don’t help much with this.
model.why: The cessation message, clearly and without moralising

model.text: I don’t know if I can just stop.

That’s fair. It’s your choice, and many people find it hard. Some get irritable, sleep badly or feel low for a few weeks after stopping. The local drug and alcohol service helps with exactly this, and you can refer yourself. Would you like the details? We can also plan it together here.
model.why: Motivational, supportive approach and referral (NICE CG51)

model.text: Yeah, give me the details. I’ll think about it.

One more thing: it’s illegal to drive with cannabis in your system, and regular use can affect your licence, so please don’t drive after using. And be careful with very hot water; people do scald themselves.

During an attack, sip fluids. If you can’t keep anything down for a day, feel dizzy or pass very little urine, or if you get green or bloody vomit or severe constant pain, get seen urgently. Can you tell me what you’re taking away?
It’s probably the weed, stopping is the cure, call the service, and get help if I can’t keep fluids down.
Spot on. Let’s meet again in a few weeks to see how you’re getting on, whatever you decide.

Persistent misuse of or dependence on cannabis must be notified to DVLA, and the person must stop driving (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).
Disclosure of drug use is confidential. Record it accurately and explain who can see the record.

Once the label is made, still reassess new or different symptoms rather than attributing everything to cannabis.

playbook.diagnosisLay: “In some people who use cannabis regularly for a long time, the body’s sickness controls get switched the wrong way, causing attacks of vomiting. Hot water seems to calm that down for a while, which is why the showers help.”

management.psychosocial: Ask without judgement, respect his choice, use a motivational approach, and warn about withdrawal.
sharedPlan: Explain that sustained cessation is the only treatment that stops the attacks

pitfalls.intro: The whole station turns on one question that previous clinicians never asked. Marks are lost by not asking about cannabis, by ordering more tests, and by lecturing once he tells you.

items.why: The syndrome is missed without a substance history, however many scans are done.
items.fix: Ask routinely and neutrally, prompted by the hot-shower clue.

items.why: Repeated normal results with a typical pattern do not need repeating unless something new appears.
items.fix: Screen red flags; investigate only new features.

items.why: Standard antiemetics often give little benefit in this syndrome.
items.fix: Make sustained cessation the treatment and give hydration advice.

items.why: Judgement ends engagement; NICE CG51 supports motivational approaches.
items.fix: Thank him, respect his choice and offer help.

items.fail: Dismissing his belief that cannabis helps.
items.fix: Acknowledge it and explain why long-term use does the opposite.

items.fail: No dehydration safety-net or driving advice.
items.why: Prolonged vomiting can cause AKI, and driving after cannabis is illegal.
items.fix: Give specific return advice and cover driving and DVLA.

avoid.instead: “Your tests have been normal several times. The pattern, especially the showers, points to a cause we can act on.”
avoid.why: Repeat investigation without asking about cannabis prolongs the cycle.

avoid.instead: “The only thing that stops these attacks is stopping cannabis. It’s your decision, and I can help if you want to try.”
avoid.why: Moralising loses engagement; a supportive, motivational approach keeps him coming back (NICE CG51).

avoid.dont: “Take these anti-sickness tablets when it starts.”
avoid.instead: “Anti-sickness tablets usually don’t help much with this. Sip fluids and get seen if you can’t keep them down.”
avoid.why: Standard antiemetics are often ineffective; the priority is hydration and cessation.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is cannabis hyperemesis syndrome: repeated vomiting attacks caused by long-term regular cannabis use.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “In some people who use cannabis regularly for a long time, the body’s sickness controls get switched the wrong way, causing attacks of vomiting. Hot water seems to calm that down for a while, which is why the showers help.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried something serious was being missed. Your tests being normal and the shower clue together give us the answer.”
management.psychosocial: Ask without judgement, respect his choice, use a motivational approach, and warn about withdrawal.
sharedPlan: Explain that sustained cessation is the only treatment that stops the attacks
Offer referral or self-referral to the local drug and alcohol service (NICE CG51)
Advice on hydration in attacks, scald risk, and driving law and DVLA
safetyNet: Unable to keep fluids down for a day, dizziness or very little urine: urgent assessment
Green or bloody vomit, severe constant pain, weight loss or new neurological symptoms: return promptly
Review in a few weeks whatever he decides

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The whole station turns on one question that previous clinicians never asked. Marks are lost by not asking about cannabis, by ordering more tests, and by lecturing once he tells you.

items.why: The syndrome is missed without a substance history, however many scans are done.
items.fix: Ask routinely and neutrally, prompted by the hot-shower clue.

items.why: Repeated normal results with a typical pattern do not need repeating unless something new appears.
items.fix: Screen red flags; investigate only new features.

items.why: Standard antiemetics often give little benefit in this syndrome.
items.fix: Make sustained cessation the treatment and give hydration advice.

items.why: Judgement ends engagement; NICE CG51 supports motivational approaches.
items.fix: Thank him, respect his choice and offer help.

items.fail: Dismissing his belief that cannabis helps.
items.fix: Acknowledge it and explain why long-term use does the opposite.

items.fail: No dehydration safety-net or driving advice.
items.why: Prolonged vomiting can cause AKI, and driving after cannabis is illegal.
items.fix: Give specific return advice and cover driving and DVLA.
